root_idea.summary: The root centrally denotes raising the head while drinking, especially stopping or refusing water.
root_idea.development: From the posture of raising the head and ceasing to drink developed expressions for aversion to water, passive restraint, and figurative refusal or pride. The wheat and dry-food branches are recorded as divergent lexical developments, while several other nouns preserve specialized uses.

qac_form_accounting.reason: Displayed under the normalized singular passive-participle citation form.

senses.definition: Having the head raised and the eyes contracted; held or left in that raised-head posture.
senses.usage_conditions: The Quranic form occurs in the plural, describing people in a passive-participial construction. The image is based on the posture of one who raises the head and ceases to drink.

senses.definition: Figuratively, obstinately refusing submission to truth, guidance, or expenditure in a good cause.
senses.usage_conditions: This is the Quran-specific figurative application of the raised-head image in 36:8, portraying refusal to yield or accept right guidance rather than introducing a separate morphological form.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To eat a dry farinaceous food, such as parched barley or wheat meal, by taking it into the mouth without moistening or kneading it.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: The action includes taking the food in the palm and conveying or licking it into the mouth; it is distinguished from eating bread, dates, and similar moist foods.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To drink a beverage, including water, milk, or nabīdh.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: This is a transitive use for drinking the named liquid or beverage.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To raise the head from water and stop or refuse drinking; also, of a person, to drink with dislike or loathing.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: The refusal may follow satiety, aversion, cold water, or illness. A disputed explanation extends the verb to becoming very languid from intense thirst, but that explanation is rejected by another authority.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To repel someone with a small or paltry thing in place of what is substantially due to him.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: The expression is used especially of an unjust distribution in which the distributor keeps the better share and gives the other party the least or meanest portion.
The name is explained by the camels' raising their heads and refusing water because of the water's coldness.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To cause someone's head to be held raised by a neck collar or shackle.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: The constricting neck-ring and its connecting bar prevent the captive from lowering the head by pressing or pricking beneath the chin.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To elevate the head out of pride; to carry the nose high and behave proudly or disdainfully.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: This is a figurative extension involving a head or nose habitually held high.

other_classical_meanings.definition: According to a disputed explanation, to render a camel very languid through severe thirst.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: The attribution is reported but explicitly treated as erroneous by another authority.

other_classical_meanings.definition: Of ears of grain or wheat, to become filled with farinaceous substance and reach maturity.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: The expression concerns the development of wheat as the floury substance fills the ears and the grain becomes mature.

other_classical_meanings.definition: Wheat, including a grain of wheat.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: The term can refer to wheat from full growth until the grain becomes compact; in the expression جَرَى القَمْحُ فِي السُّنْبُلِ, the farinaceous substance has pervaded the ears. The word is particularly associated with Syrian usage, though it is also reported elsewhere.

other_classical_meanings.definition: A mouthful of dry food taken into the mouth; according to some, a mouthful of water.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: The food sense refers to the material eaten in the manner of dry intake described under قَمِحَهُ.
This is an anatomical noun with the two recorded lexical forms.

other_classical_meanings.definition: The part between the occiput and the small hollow at the back of the neck.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A specific anatomical designation for the upper back of the neck.

other_classical_meanings.definition: A name for wars, a perfume, saffron, or the froth or white surface substance that forms on wine.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: The lexicographical identifications vary; the wine sense is described as a scum resembling the perfume called dharīrah.

other_classical_meanings.definition: Aversion of a camel from drinking.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: The aversion is attributed to satisfied thirst, loathing, cold water, or illness; the expression شَهْرَا قُمَاحٍ names the coldest months from this behavior.

other_classical_meanings.definition: A great drinker of nabīdh or a similar beverage.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: Used adjectivally of a person characterized by heavy drinking.

other_classical_meanings.definition: Food eaten dry by taking it into the mouth without moistening, especially parched barley or wheat meal; also a digestive preparation.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: The term may also describe dry herbage that camels take into the mouth unmoistened or lick up.

other_classical_meanings.definition: A camel that raises its head from water and refuses to drink, or dislikes water.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: The adjective applies to either a male or female camel. A disputed explanation also uses it for a camel made languid by severe thirst.

cautions: The sole Quran occurrence is the plural passive participle مُقْمَحُونَ; the public headword is normalized to the singular citation form مُقْمَحٌ.

The interpretation of 36:8 includes both the raised-head image and its figurative application to refusal of guidance; an additional interpretation associates the posture with shackles in the hereafter, which is interpretive context rather than a separate lexical sense.

Several Classical extensions involving languor from thirst are explicitly reported as disputed and have been retained as attributed variants rather than presented as the primary water-aversion meaning.
